title: The attraction of stride piano
summary: Discussing his Thou Swell performance, he says stride's left hand grabbed him from the start, likening its pulse to the heart and lungs.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well you got me with your “Thou Swell.” I mean even from a rhythmic drive, like wow, that made my heart speed up a little bit I think.
That stride thing, I just like well that’s almost impossible what you’re doing.

Well you know I mean the stride was I think what got me the most since the very beginning, even when I started playing classical and I didn’t know about the existence of jazz. When I would hear someone play that thing with the left hand, I don’t know what it was it would just get to me, you know? I don’t know if someone would say what is it that got your attention about that left hand? I liked it. You know? I just felt it in my stomach. You know? I don’t know. To me one possible explanation is that, that movement of the left hand, bass and chord, oomp pa, oomp pa, oomp pa. In a certain way resembles the very meaning of life, that is the pulse of your heart. You know? The opening and closing of your lungs. So probably at a subconscious level I associate that with the very basic function of life that makes our lives as human beings possible. The rhythmic contraction of the heart and the lungs. That’s the only explanation I can give about this sort of attraction I always felt.
Well it got me in the heart.
